cards.title: Use the Shopping List Test to Diagnose Brand Dilution
cards.summary: A quick test for whether your brand name means one thing or many, by asking what a spouse would bring back from a written shopping list.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a new product category, sub-brand, or SKU under your existing store/brand name, or evaluating whether an existing catalog is already diluted.
steps: Write down your brand name alone on a list, the way a customer would. Ask: if someone read just this name, is there exactly one product they would return with?

Contrast with strong names: 'Kleenex', 'Bayer', and 'Dial' pass because they map to one product each. 'Heinz', 'Scott', and 'Kraft' fail because the reader cannot tell whether they mean ketchup, pickles, or baby food.
Apply this to your own catalog: list your brand plus each category you sell under that same name. If customers cannot predict the product from the name alone, the name has no independent position.

Note the source's claim that the damage is slow and cumulative — the brand becomes a 'burned-out hulk' over years, not quarters, so a single successful quarter of extension sales does not disprove the problem.
Treat 'what's a [brand]?' as the diagnostic question: if the answer is 'it's everything and nothing', you have a positioning problem to fix before extending further.
caveats: The source is a 1980s packaged-goods argument; its share-loss examples are illustrative, not benchmarks for your store.
A broad house name works fine for low-involvement commodity items where shoppers have no going-in preference — the test matters most where you want to own a category.

cards.title: Line Extension's Short-Term Sales Illusion
cards.summary: New line extensions create an instant recognition flash and pipeline sales that look strong for months, then fade when reorders do not come.
cards.use_when: Interpreting early sales data after launching a new SKU under an existing brand name, or setting expectations with a founder before a sub-brand launch.
steps: Recognize that a name related to the original ('Diet Coca-Cola', 'Alka-Seltzer Plus') produces an instant flash of understanding and an instant flash of sales.

Separate pipeline from demand: retail buyers stocking the new SKU produce good numbers in the first months regardless of consumer pull. The source notes that booking $1 million only requires $35 of stocking per supermarket.
Watch the reorder curve as the real signal. When reorders do not arrive, the source says things turn dark quickly.
Expect the extended name to be forgettable because it has no independent position — the source calls such names satellites to the original, contributing only blur.
For an online store, the analog is a variant or bundle launched under a hero product's name: check repeat purchase and direct search for the new item, not just launch-week sell-through.
caveats: The '$35 per supermarket' figure is the source's illustrative arithmetic for physical retail distribution, not a benchmark for ecommerce.
Anti-extension argument, not a blanket ban; the source explicitly allows extension when there is no competition and no intention to build a position.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Bayer and Protein 21: How Sub-Brands Undercut the Parent
cards.summary: Every extension hung on a strong brand erodes the parent's meaning, shown in falling share for Bayer analgesics and Protein 21 shampoo.
cards.use_when: Considering whether to attach your main brand name to an adjacent product line, ingredient variant, or differently-positioned version.
steps: Apply the contradiction test: if the brand means aspirin, 'Bayer nonaspirin' cannot logically exist in the customer's mind. Each extension — timed-release, decongestant, nonaspirin — undercuts the aspirin position.
Track the share consequence the source reports: Bayer's total analgesic share kept falling as the line extended.

Use Protein 21 as the cautionary arc: a shampoo/conditioner that reached a 13% share of the shampoo market, then extended into hairspray, conditioner, concentrate, and Protein 29 for men, and fell to 2%.
Translate to a store: if your brand means one ingredient or one job, do not put that name on a product with a contradictory job. Give the new job a new name.
Treat the share declines as the source's historical examples, and check your own category data before concluding extension caused it.
caveats: Share figures are historical packaged-goods examples from the source, not predictive benchmarks.
The source also warns the decline is 'bound to continue' — an opinion about trajectory, worth testing rather than assuming.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Broadening the Base: Reverse Line Extension
cards.summary: Same product, same package, same name — only the use occasion changes, which is how Johnson's baby shampoo became an adult brand.
cards.use_when: Looking for growth from an existing hero product without launching a new SKU, or planning messaging and landing-page angles for a narrowly perceived product.
steps: Identify a product whose current perception limits its audience but whose actual attributes fit a bigger one. Johnson's baby shampoo was promoted for its mildness to the adult market and became a leading adult shampoo.
Keep product, package, and label unchanged. The source states that a separate 'Johnson's adult shampoo' extension would not have been nearly as successful.

Find the sole unclaimed usage claim, as Blue Nun did by advertising a white wine as good with meat as well as fish. The source argues these work because each is the first and only brand making that claim.
Apply to ecommerce: rewrite PDP copy, ad creative, and use-case imagery to promote the additional occasion or audience for the same SKU, rather than creating a duplicate listing under a new name.
Check that no competitor already owns the broadened claim before investing; the source attributes the success partly to being first with it.
caveats: Source's examples are beverages and personal care; the mechanism (usage broadening) transfers, the results do not.
Advertising-intensive: the source ties these wins to sustained promotion, so a silent PDP edit alone is unlikely to shift perception.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: The Bartender Test for Step-Up and Step-Down Products
cards.summary: Premium and entry-price variants built on a value name create confusion and weak sales at the premium end except when the buyer can name them without the parent.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a premium tier or a cheaper entry model should carry your existing brand name, and how to name tiers in a catalog or subscription ladder.
steps: Run the bartender test on your own brand: order it the way a customer would. 'J&B on the rocks' reliably gets scotch; 'Chivas' reliably gets the premium version. 'Cutty' does not tell the bartender whether you mean Cutty Sark or Cutty 12.

For step-up products, the source observes they usually produce anemic sales at the higher price — buyers do not want to pay premium prices for a low-price name. Chivas Regal outsold the earlier Johnnie Walker Black Label.

For step-down products, the source observes near-instant success followed by a hangover: Packard's inexpensive Clipper was its best-selling car and destroyed the prestige position that kept the company alive.

The exception: Vaseline Intensive Care works because customers simply call the product 'Intensive Care' — in the mind, Vaseline is petroleum jelly and Intensive Care is hand lotion. A separate name in the customer's mouth is what saves it.
Store application: name premium tiers so customers can say the tier name alone, and avoid slapping the hero brand on a cheap entry SKU that pays the bills short-term but erodes pricing power.
caveats: The step-up and step-down patterns are the source's observations from liquor and autos, stated as tendencies, not laws.
The Vaseline case shows extension can survive when the extension name is what people actually say — verify this through customer language, not internal naming documents.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: When to Use the House Name: Five Rules of the Road
cards.summary: The source's five criteria for deciding whether a new product should carry the existing house brand or get its own name.
cards.use_when: Deciding naming and brand architecture for a new product launch, collection, or private-label item in a multi-product catalog.
steps: Expected volume: potential winners should not bear the house name; small-volume products should.
Competition: in a vacuum a brand should not bear the house name; in a crowded field it should.
Advertising support: big-budget brands should not bear the house name; small-budget brands should.
Significance: breakthrough products should not bear the house name; commodity products such as chemicals should.
Distribution: off-the-shelf items should not bear the house name; items sold by sales reps should.

Note the underlying reasoning: products with no going-in preference in the shopper's mind will do better under any known name than an unknown one, and companies with thousands of small-volume products cannot afford a new name for each.
Store translation: a flagship, ad-supported, differentiated hero SKU likely earns its own name; a long-tail commodity SKU can ride the house name.
caveats: These are the source's stated heuristics, framed as 'an economics call as much as a judgment call' — apply with your own volume and margin data.
The rules assume a world where advertising budget and distribution channel differ by product; re-derive them for your channel mix.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: First-Mover Position and the 100mm Cigarette
cards.summary: Being first into a new product concept is worthless if the name does not claim the concept — a competitor with a clearer name can preempt the position.
cards.use_when: You are early into a new product category, format, or claim and choosing how to name and describe it in your store and ads.
steps: Identify whether you are genuinely first with a new concept, format, or benefit, as Pall Mall Gold was the first 100mm cigarette and Mazola was the first corn-oil margarine.

Do not dilute the first-mover claim by attaching the incumbent house name to it. The source argues Pall Mall's line-extension thinking let Benson & Hedges preempt the long-cigarette position, and Fleischmann's now leads corn-oil margarine.

Name the new concept so the name itself carries the idea. Taster's Choice beat Maxim 2-to-1 even though General Foods invented freeze-dried coffee, partly because 'Maxim' connoted nothing and 'Taster's Choice' plus 'tastes like ground roast' related the product to a standard of excellence.
Apply the same to a store: a genuinely new format or benefit deserves a distinct, benefit-connoting name and copy, not a variant SKU of a legacy bestseller.
Watch the share trajectory after extending: Pall Mall went from No. 1 in 1964 with 14.4% share to 3.8%, per the source, following its first extension in 1965.
caveats: All share figures are the source's historical examples, not forecasts for your category.
The source acknowledges that leading brands like Marlboro and Winston also extended — it frames the outcome as a tendency, not an inevitability.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: The Three-Act Pattern of a Positioned Brand's Decline
cards.summary: A breakthrough brand often loses its position by extending into adjacent models, as Volkswagen fell from first to fourth among imports.
cards.use_when: Reviewing an expanding product line or variant count, or planning a range extension for a category-leading product.
steps: Act One: a big breakthrough from finding a wide-open slot and exploiting it — Volkswagen with 'Think small' and the small-car position. The source notes the brand rose above name to become a lifestyle statement for a practical, no-nonsense buyer.
Act Two: greed and visions of unending success lead to extending the same reliability and quality to bigger, more expensive cars, buses, and jeep-type vehicles.
Act Three: the reversal. The source reports Volkswagen fell from first among imported cars to fourth, behind Toyota, Datsun, and Honda.
Diagnose your own line: count the models or variants carrying the hero name. The source asks whether eight models can sell as well as one — and answers that in this case they did not.
Use 'what's a [brand]?' on your own expanded line. If the answer is 'a big, small, cheap, expensive car' (the source's Chevrolet critique), the range has entered the everybody trap.
If breadth is needed, the source's alternative is a new concept with a new position and a new name.
caveats: The Volkswagen decline is the source's example, with its own era's competitive context, not a general law about range width.
Range breadth can be right for some retailers; the source's argument targets brands attempting to own a position in the customer's mind.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Name as Rubber Band: How Far to Stretch
cards.summary: A brand name stretches only so far before weakening, so decide extension scope by category economics and by whether a focused competitor can out-position you.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many product categories one brand name should cover, versus launching a separate brand or holding a category-specific name.
steps: Accept that the stretch limit is an economics question, not purely a judgment call: putting a separate name on peas, corn, and string beans would not be economical, so Del Monte using one name across canned fruits and vegetables is probably right.
Watch for the focused attacker. Dole versus Del Monte in canned pineapple is, in the source's words, 'no contest' — the specialist wins.
Run the teeter-totter check: if Dole makes the name mean bananas, what happens to the pineapple franchise? Extending one meaning trades against another.

Decide consciously whether you want full-line supplier status or a category franchise. The source says Dole can become full-line only at the expense of its valuable pineapple franchise, and with the added disadvantage of being the last to extend.
For a store: if a category has a credible specialist competitor, holding a category-specific name or sub-brand for that category protects the position better than folding it into a general brand.
caveats: Del Monte and Dole conclusions are the source's market observations, not universal rules.
The source explicitly tolerates broad names for commodities with no meaningful brand preference.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Diagnose Star Products Whose Sales Outrun Their Position
cards.summary: A product can lead a market it does not own in the customer's mind — Jergens Extra Dry lost to Intensive Care because the name did not convey the difference.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether a category-leading SKU in your catalog actually owns a distinct claim, or launching an innovation that looks like a variant of an existing product.
steps: Separate market share from share of mind, as the source does for Scott: leading the paper-products market did not mean owning a position, and Charmin eventually displaced ScotTissue.
Test whether the customer can name which product does which job: the source asks which brand is engineered for the nose, Scotties or ScotTissue — the answer is unclear, so the name sits in limbo.

When you have a real innovation hidden inside a familiar name, rename it. Jergens Extra Dry was a creamlike lotion in an era of liquid lotions, but the similar name meant prospects did not recognize the difference; Chesebrough-Pond's Intensive Care named and positioned it clearly and took the lead.

Watch for the specialist's opening: if a competitor clearly names and positions the difference you buried, the source says the marketing victory goes to them, and a late counter-brand (Direct Aid) may be too little, too late.
Even a line-extended winner here is called by its extension name — customers say 'Intensive Care', not 'Vaseline' — so check what customers actually call your product.
caveats: History is the source's packaged-goods examples, not a measured forecast.
The lesson is about distinct position, not merely renaming: a rename without a real, communicated difference will not carry the position.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Position the Destination, Not the Vehicle (Country and Company Positioning)
cards.summary: Sabena could not sell flights to a country nobody wanted to visit, so the productive move was positioning Belgium as a destination first.
cards.use_when: Marketing a marketplace, region, or store category where demand must be grown before your own product can sell, including multi-seller marketplace or regional seller positioning.
steps: Find the destination-level problem before optimizing your own offer. Sabena sold food and service while only one in fifty North Atlantic passengers flew to Belgium at all; the source argues no amount of food advertising induces a flight to somewhere the traveler does not want to go.
Do what KLM had done for Amsterdam: make the place a destination people want to spend time in, rather than a place they pass through.
Build the position on a perception already in the prospect's mind. The 'three-star cities of beautiful Belgium' campaign anchored to Amsterdam, which travelers already knew.
Borrow credibility from an authority already trusted. The source credits the Michelin Guide (which rated five Belgian cities three-star 'worth a special journey') with making the claim believable.

Make the offer sufficient for a multi-day decision. The source notes nobody treats Monaco as a destination because Monte Carlo can be seen in an evening — five cities made Belgium a bona fide destination.
For a store: if your category requires a habit or occasion the customer does not yet have, market the occasion, then your product as the best execution of it.
caveats: The Belgium program, per the source, was not ultimately executed because new management did not commit — the source treats that as its own lesson about long-term commitment.
This is an agency case from the source's era; the transferable mechanism is anchoring to existing perceptions, not the specific media plan.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Avoid Cliché Visuals That Blur Your Category
cards.summary: Beaches-and-palms visuals for every Caribbean island get dumped in one mental slot, so use a distinctive visual device tied to your specific position.
cards.use_when: Planning ad creative, PDP imagery, or a landing-page hero where your category's visuals look identical to competitors'.
steps: Audit your category's standard imagery. The source notes the couple on the beach under palms is a visual cliché for the Caribbean, and asks whether a customer can keep Nassau, the Virgin Islands, and Barbados separate in mind. If not, the mind files them under 'islands' and tunes out.
Break with the cliché using something already meaningful, as Jamaica's neighbor Bermuda did with motorbikes beside pink sand — an enduring, effective visual.
Design a distinctive device that carries your position's meaning. For Belgium, Michelin stars were used as if they were church bells ringing as they were superimposed on city scenes.

Reach for moving image when the position is visual: the source says television drives pictures of a place into the mind faster than print. Adapt for ecommerce by using video where the position is pictorial.
Warn against the same blur in other formats: quaint European villages or smiling residents waving mugs of beer fail for the same reason as the palms.
caveats: The Bermuda visual is cited as effective and long-running, not as a measured lift.
The Belgium television work is described by the source as generating substantial response, but the program was not fully deployed — treat response as directional.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Positioning Must Be Sustained by Committed Management
cards.summary: A positioning program lives or dies on a long-term commitment from the people in charge, not on the quality of the concept alone.
cards.use_when: Setting positioning or rebranding direction for a store and deciding how to protect it through team, agency, or platform changes.
steps: Treat positioning as a multi-year commitment. The source's Belgium program failed not because the concept was weak but because new management arrived uncommitted and headquarters changed strategy.
Write the position down with the reasoning and the evidence (the shopping-list test result, the anchor perception, the credibility source) so a successor inherits the argument, not just the slogan.
Note the source's own framing: whether it's a corporation, a church, an airline, or a country, a successful positioning program requires major long-term commitment by the people in charge.
Build in a re-check rather than a rewrite: the source says you must constantly keep your position targeted to today's problems and today's markets, which is different from abandoning it for fashion.
For an ecommerce operator with high founder or agency turnover, document the position in the brand guide and tie creative, naming, and range decisions to it.
caveats: The source's evidence is a case study where the program was abandoned; it demonstrates the risk, not a measured effect of commitment.
The source acknowledges this is difficult in a constantly changing political environment — the same applies to fast-changing platform and marketing environments.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Third-Leg Strategy: Grow From the Position You Own
cards.summary: Rather than fighting a leader on their turf, Xerox's opportunity was to extend its copier position into the adjacent output lane it already owned.
cards.use_when: Deciding which adjacent category, product line, or feature set to enter when your store already owns one strong position and a bigger competitor owns the adjacent one.
steps: Map the market as legs. The office had three: telephones (AT&T), typewriters/computers (IBM), and copiers (Xerox). Ask which leg you currently own and whether new technology has changed what that leg means.
Do not attack the leg you do not own. The source notes Xerox failed at computers, workstations, and local area networks (IBM's leg), and IBM failed at copiers (Xerox's leg).
Find what your own leg has become. The copier leg of the future is the output leg: printers, scanners, storage devices.

Look for a technology that has already earned credibility elsewhere to attach to that leg — the laser, in the source's account, had proven itself in communication, medicine, retail checkout, and consumer disk players.

Name the new capability so it connects to your existing meaning: 'lasography' sounds new and different, sounds related to xerography, and uses a leading-edge technology, so it broadens the existing position instead of abandoning it.

For a store: extend from your owned position outward (e.g., from one category you genuinely own into adjacent formats for the same job), not into a category where a dominant specialist already owns the customer's mind.
caveats: Xerox's attempts are recounted as failures by the source; this is a strategic proposal made at the time, not a documented success.
The leg framework reflects that era's office market; the reasoning about avoiding the leader's turf transfers, the specific technologies do not.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Corporate Clarity: What Does Your Company Name Stand For?
cards.summary: A company name should stand for something specific inside its industry, since diversification and 'our people' are weak corporate positioning platforms.
cards.use_when: Positioning your store or company as a whole — for recruiting, supplier relationships, or investor conversations— rather than positioning one product.
steps: Check whether your name locks you to a past reputation. The source notes Pullman is barely a factor in railroad cars and Greyhound's buses keep it perceptually stuck despite millions telling the financial community it is 'more than a bus company'. If you want a broader meaning, the source argues you need a new name, not corporate advertising against the existing one.
Pick a quality that cuts across all your offerings, as Ford settled on 'innovation' ('Ford has a better idea') since it builds all types and sizes.

Avoid a people-based platform. The source argues most people assume bigger, more successful companies have better people, so claiming better people from a non-top position creates an inconsistency the prospect resolves against you.

Avoid 'diversification' as the theme. The source states positions are built on major achievements, not broad product lines, and cites GE as known for electrical manufacturing rather than diversified goods — plus stock markets undervaluing conglomerates.

Beware positions so broad they are meaningless: the source cites a company describing itself as 'a developer and supplier of information systems for work, education, and entertainment' — Bell & Howell.
Apply to a store: if you cannot state what your company name means in one specific way inside your category, tighten it before recruiting or supplier campaigns.
caveats: These are the source's observations about corporate advertising platforms, offered as strong opinions ('diversification is not the answer').
The Pullman and Greyhound examples are historical; verify current brand facts before citing them.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Find the Mental Postcard Before Shooting New Imagery
cards.summary: If one image perfectly captured your product's essence, someone would already have used it — so search for the existing perception rather than hunting a new shot.
cards.use_when: Planning brand photography, a category hero image, or creative territory for a store whose category visuals are interchangeable with competitors'.
steps: Start from perceptions already in the prospect's mind, not from a blank creative brief. In the travel case, countries are stored as mental picture postcards — England as pageantry and Big Ben, Amsterdam as tulips and canals, New York as a skyline.

Do not begin by sorting existing imagery for the one perfect picture. The source's reasoning is decisive: if one image captured the essence of the island, someone would have noticed and used it, meaning an image would already be burned into some minds.
Do not begin by shooting hundreds or thousands of new photos either. In the Jamaica case, the source reports that nothing totally right turned up from that approach.
Instead, locate the strongest existing perception or authority claim and build the visual system around it — as the Belgium work anchored to Amsterdam and borrowed Michelin's stars.

For a store: before commissioning a shoot, ask which image your customers already associate with your product's job, then produce imagery that sharpens that association rather than a generic category shot.
caveats: The Jamaica passage is where the source's extract ends; the resolution of that search is not stated here.
The insight is about search method (existing perception first), not proof that new photography can never work.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx
